body.text: Beijing Scan is ORF’s monthly insight on China, analysing crucial political, economic, foreign policy, and military developments.

• China’s economy is strong, but increasingly imbalanced. Record exports and widening surpluses reveal manufacturing strength, but weak domestic demand and slower growth expose the export-led model’s limits.
• India-China ties are thawing, but the core problems remain. Diplomatic, military and economic engagement is expanding, but border tensions, trade deficits and Chinese non-tariff barriers persist.

• China is turning military hardware into operational experience. Three air exercises diversify training partners, platforms and environments, narrowing experience gaps and enhancing interoperability.

Chinese exports surged 25 percent year-on-year in August 2026, driven by strong demand for automobiles and high-tech products, as the country’s record trade surplus widened further. China’s imports from the world rose 28.2 percent year-on-year in August, up from July’s 27.5 percent increase. The trade surplus expanded to US$119.1 billion in August from US$112.5 billion in July. Customs data showed that automobile exports increased 43 percent year-on-year in August, while semiconductor exports surged 129.8 percent.
Image 1: China’s August 2026 Trade
Source: Reuters

Chinese shipments to the United States rose 34.4 percent year-on-year in August, extending the double-digit growth recorded for most of the year, while imports from the United States increased 17.8 percent. Exports to the European Union grew 6.6 percent, while imports from the bloc increased 0.7 percent. In August, China’s imports from South Korea more than doubled, while exports jumped nearly 50 percent.

Beijing has set a target range of 4.5–5 percent for China’s GDP growth in 2026. Although economic growth remained strong at the start of the year, it slowed to 4.3 percent in the second quarter — its weakest pace in more than three years.
Figure 1: China’s Economy in August 2026
Source: Author-created with assistance from ChatGPT 5.5

China’s exorbitant surplus is fuelling calls from several countries for Beijing to allow the yuan to appreciate. Critics argue that the currency’s undervaluation has contributed to China’s export boom. China’s export boom is also drawing scrutiny from Western trading partners, which are pressing Beijing to rebalance its trade and boost domestic demand.

China’s rising exports and growing trade surplus became a source of controversy at the G20 meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors in Asheville, North Carolina. The G20 chair’s statement, issued on 1 September 2026, said that 19 of 20 participating members agreed to address economic imbalances and eliminate non-market policies. China was the lone dissenting member. United States (US) Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described China’s trade surplus as a barrier to global economic growth and called for Beijing to rebalance its economy away from exports and towards domestic consumption.

The Chinese government has accelerated fiscal spending in recent weeks to arrest the decline in investment and restore economic stability. Beijing is also preparing a US$ 54 billion capital injection into several state-owned banks and insurers as it seeks to bolster growth through targeted fiscal support.

The package will strengthen the capital bases of three major state-owned banks and five insurers, including the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the Agricultural Bank of China and China Life Insurance. The move marks Beijing’s latest effort to reinvigorate the economy amid trade tensions with the West, ongoing wars, weak domestic demand and an ageing population.

On 25 August, India’s National Security Advisor Ajit Doval met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing for the 25th round of Special Representatives (SR) negotiations. The SR framework was established to resolve the boundary question from a political perspective. The Joint Communique, ‘Eight Points of Outcomes and Consensus’, released after the talks, covered several crucial issues, including border trade cooperation, increasing the size and number of pilgrim groups, transboundary rivers and hydrological data sharing, and peace in the border areas. The Chinese readout reiterated the importance of placing the boundary issue in its appropriate place to create a “positive narrative” [正面叙事].

The joint communique mentioned the establishment of an Expert Group on Boundary Delimitation and another Working Group on Border Management under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (WMCC) to advance discussions on the ‘early and substantial harvest’ of boundary delimitation and border management. China had proposed an ‘Early Harvest’ in 2017 negotiations after the Doklam Standoff. India rejected the proposal, as the Middle Sector of the Line of Actual Control (LAC) is relatively clear, but the two trijunctions between India, Tibet, and Bhutan at Batang La and between India, Tibet, and Nepal in Lipulekh remain contested. New Delhi instead offered a counterproposal under which border issues would be discussed as a package through an ‘early and substantial harvest’ proposal. China appears to have agreed to this approach during the 2026 SR talks, although the terms of reference are yet to be negotiated.
Figure 2: The 25th India-China SR Talks

In the military domain, the Indian Army and the PLA are engaging at the unit level through border personnel meetings (BPMs) at five places, at the senior-most commander level at four places including Kibithu and are establishing hotlines between their Central and Eastern Army Commands. The effort is to maintain peace along the border, as any renewed disturbance could undermine the cautious rapprochement achieved so far.

In the economic domain, Press Note 3 has relaxed criteria for investment in non-strategic sectors, allowed joint-venture formations, and permitted Chinese foreign portfolio investment (FPI) entry if the share is non-controlling and up to 10 percent. India has also allowed the time-bound resolution of investment proposals from China in sectors such as capital goods, electronic components, polysilicon, and ingot wafers. Chinese firms with manufacturing units in India have even been allowed to participate in government tenders for power projects.
Figure 3: India-China Cautious Engagement

Border trade at three points has also resumed. Nevertheless, the large trade deficit of US$ 112 billion and the predatory mercantile nature of China’s exports remain a core Indian concern. New Delhi has been seeking market access in China for products such as pharmaceuticals and marine products; however, the application of non-tariff barriers to constrain Indian export prospects remains a major concern. Moreover, China has recently restricted business visas for Indian engineers and technicians, including those working for Indian joint-venture companies, affecting the operations of Indian firms dependent on Chinese suppliers.

In the last month, China's PLA has conducted a series of military exercises with friendly forces. The People's Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) held the fourth iteration of the Swift Eagle 2026 airborne exercise with Belarus at the PLA Air Force Training Centre in Hubei Province from 12 to 24 August 2026. The exercise included parachute operations using IL-76, Y-9, and Y-20 aircraft; unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and counter-UAV training; live-fire exercises; and fast-roping from Z-20 helicopters.
Image 2: China-Belarus Joint Airborne Exercise 2026
Source: China Military Online

In addition, a PLA Air Force contingent comprising J-16 fighters, Y-20 aircraft, helicopters, among other assets, arrived in Egypt on 21 August 2026 to participate in the second edition of the Eagles of Civilisation 2026 exercises, which ran until early September. The two forces sought to share their expertise in air combat tactics, air superiority operations, combat search and rescue, and joint mission planning and force employment during the exercise.
Image 3: China-Egypt Joint Air Exercise 2026
Source: The Egyptian Gazette
Image 4: Eagles of Civilisation Exercise 2026
Source: Ahram Online

Additionally, from 10 to 20 August, the Chinese and Thai air forces held the ninth edition of Falcon Strike 2026, a joint air exercise in Thailand, primarily at airbases near Udon Thani and Bangkok. The PLAAF deployed J-10C, J-10S, and Y-20 aircraft, along with airborne early-warning and refuelling aircraft and ground-based air defence units, among others, to exercise with Thai air assets, including Gripen fighters and Alpha Jet trainers. The exercise focused on joint air defence, force deployment, and humanitarian and medical rescue operations.
Image 5: China-Thai Joint Air Exercise 2026

The PLAAF has been rapidly expanding and upgrading both the size and sophistication of its inventory. It now operates more than 300 J-20 stealth fighters and roughly 1,500 fourth- and fourth-plus-generation fighters, including the J-16, J-11, J-10, Su-30 and Su-35 families, alongside combat-enabling platforms.
Figure 4: China’s Joint Air Exercises in August 2026

Personnel quality and operational experience, however, remain more difficult to generate at the same pace as hardware. The PLAAF has therefore used regular international exercises, especially with Pakistan, Thailand, the UAE and Egypt, to expose its personnel to unfamiliar operational environments, tactics, command procedures and air-combat practices.

These air forces maintain extensive operational relationships and, in several cases, regularly train with Western air forces. Such engagements can help China observe and test different approaches to air combat, mission planning, interoperability and operational command—areas that cannot be fully replicated through domestic training. As its capabilities mature, Beijing will seek additional exercise partners and training environments to expose its personnel to diverse and demanding forms of air warfare.

Scarborough Shoal has become a focal point in the South China Sea as China seeks to strengthen its control over the disputed feature and the surrounding region. In September 2025, Beijing established the Huangyan Island National Nature Reserve, covering the shoal and nearby waters. On 1 August 2026, China issued regulations managing the reserve, banning illegal fishing and poaching, preventing acts that damage the environment, and establishing regular patrols.
Image 6: Zhongsha Islands
Source: Sentinel Vision

In August 2026, China also approved the construction of the Zhongsha Islands (including Scarborough Shoal and Macclesfield Bank) Marine Ecological and Environmental Field Observation and Research Station. The proposed station will establish a three-dimensional, multilayered marine observation network of sea-based dual-core and land-based logistics and consolidate China's administrative presence in the disputed South China Sea.
Image 7: Teodoro at Seoul Defence Dialogue 2026
Source: Observer News Network

As discussed in the previous Beijing Scan, Manila has countered China's legal warfare with legal instruments of its own. In July 2026, the Philippines submitted its official National Mapping and Resource Information Authority (NAMRIA) Chart No. 1567, titled Bajo de Masinloc and Approach, which incensed Beijing. Further, Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., while attending a security forum in Seoul, received a note from a Chinese embassy representative and responded by accusing China of using coercion, bullying, and aggression, as well as violating the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), of which it is a signatory. Beijing may use the episode to stoke nationalist sentiments against Manila and justify further armed coercion by the China Coast Guard and other security agencies.
